title: Check yourself: introduction to the Streams API

questions.stem: A nightly job runs `invoices.stream().map(inv -> { if (inv.disputed()) invoices.add(creditNote(inv)); return inv; }).forEach(mailer::send);` over an ArrayList of six invoices. Only the third invoice is disputed. What happens?

options.text: All six invoices are mailed, then ConcurrentModificationException is thrown, since the list's change is detected once the traversal ends
options.says: for forEach, ArrayList's spliterator compares the modification count after the last element, so every original element is processed before the exception

options.text: All six invoices are mailed, then the credit note is mailed too, since the stream reads the list as each element is pulled
options.says: a change made while the terminal operation runs is interference: the added element is not traversed, and the operation ends in ConcurrentModificationException

options.text: Two invoices are mailed, then ConcurrentModificationException is thrown, since add() refuses to change a list that a stream is reading
options.says: the add succeeds; the exception comes from the spliterator, not from the list's add

options.text: Three invoices are mailed, then ConcurrentModificationException is thrown, since the stream checks the list after each element
options.says: the check after each element happens in a short-circuiting operation; forEach checks once, after the last element

origin.section: The Source Is Read When the Terminal Operation Runs, and Must Not Change Under It

questions.stem: A scheduler builds `Stream<Job> due = jobs.stream().filter(Job::isDue);` and passes it to another method, which first appends a due job loaded from the database to `jobs` (an ArrayList) and then calls `due.toList()`. What does the call return?

options.text: The due jobs including the appended one, since the list is read when toList() starts and not when stream() was called
options.says: ArrayList's spliterator is late-binding: it binds to the elements at the first traversal, which begins with the terminal operation

options.text: The due jobs including the appended one, since an ArrayList may be appended to at any point while a stream over it runs
options.says: a change while the terminal operation runs is interference and ends in ConcurrentModificationException; this append happened before it started

options.text: The due jobs without the appended one, since stream() copies the list's elements at the moment it is called
options.says: an ArrayList stream copies nothing; the snapshot behaviour belongs to CopyOnWriteArrayList

options.text: No list: the call throws ConcurrentModificationException, since the list was changed after stream() was called
options.says: a change made before the terminal operation starts is allowed and is seen

origin.section: The Source Is Read When the Terminal Operation Runs, and Must Not Change Under It

questions.stem: `keys` holds eight cache keys. `keys.stream().map(cache::load).filter(v -> v.size() > 100).findFirst()` runs, and of the eight values only the third one is larger than 100. How many times is `load` called?

options.text: Three times, since each key goes through load and the filter before the next key is pulled
options.says: elements travel one at a time through every stage, and findFirst stops pulling once the third value passes the filter

options.text: Eight times, since map loads every key before the filter sees the first value
options.says: stages do not run one after the other over the whole list; each element goes through all of them before the next is pulled

options.text: Once, since findFirst lets only the first key through to load
options.says: findFirst stops at the first element that reaches it, which is the first value to pass the filter, so the first two keys are loaded too

options.text: Eight times, since the filter needs every loaded value before findFirst can tell which match comes first
options.says: the source is pulled in order, so the first match to arrive is the first one; findFirst needs nothing after it

origin.section: Each Element Goes Through the Whole Pipeline Before the Next, and Short-Circuiting Stops the Pulling

questions.stem: An order service's `recent()` returns `recentOrders`, a `Stream<Order>` field built when the service starts. A controller builds `late = recent().filter(Order::isLate)` and then `paid = recent().filter(Order::isPaid)`, and then calls `late.count()`. What happens?

options.text: Building `paid` throws IllegalStateException, since the stream it is called on is already linked to the `late` pipeline
options.says: any second operation that builds on the same Stream object throws, intermediate ones included, before anything has run

options.text: Both pipelines are built and `late.count()` succeeds, since no terminal operation has run on the field's stream yet
options.says: the check is not limited to terminal operations: the second filter on the same stream throws

options.text: Both pipelines are built and `late.count()` succeeds, since recent() hands out a fresh view of the orders on every call
options.says: recent() returns the same stored Stream object each time; a stream is not a view that can be handed out again

options.text: `late.count()` throws IllegalStateException, since building the field's stream at startup already used it up
options.says: building a pipeline runs nothing, and the field's stream is first used by the late pipeline's filter; it is the second filter call that throws

origin.section: A Stream Can Be Consumed Once, So Keep a Supplier, Not the Stream
